justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift across all three horizons, anchored near the prevailing price level at the time of the forecast. For the one-day estimate, I leaned heavily on short-term momentum and mean-reversion tendencies, expecting little deviation from the most recent closing price. The one-week estimate incorporates a slight positive bias consistent with a gradual trend, while the one-month estimate reflects a longer-run drift assumption — perhaps tied to underlying earnings growth expectations or broader index trends — producing only a small incremental increase over the four-week window. The relatively flat trajectory across horizons suggests I was not anticipating any major catalyst in the near term and was essentially forecasting continuation of a stable, mildly bullish regime.

The confidence interval widths widen appropriately as the horizon extends, reflecting the well-established principle that uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, the interval is quite narrow because intraday and overnight price moves tend to be bounded absent breaking news. At one week, I incorporated the possibility of scheduled economic releases, earnings announcements, or Federal Reserve communications that could shift sentiment meaningfully in either direction. By one month, the interval nearly doubles in width, acknowledging that a broader range of macroeconomic developments, geopolitical events, or sector rotation could materially alter the price trajectory.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside my stated intervals. On the downside, an unexpected hawkish policy signal, a disappointing earnings report from a heavily weighted constituent, or a sudden deterioration in credit or liquidity conditions could easily breach the lower bound, particularly at the one-month horizon. On the upside, a surprise dovish pivot, a better-than-expected inflation print, or a strong earnings beat could drive prices above my upper bounds. Tail risks such as geopolitical escalation, a flash crash triggered by algorithmic activity, or a sudden liquidity event represent lower-probability scenarios that my intervals do not fully capture by construction, since 90% intervals leave 10% of outcomes unaccounted for.

It is also worth noting that my intervals assume relatively normal market conditions and roughly log-normal return distributions. In practice, financial returns exhibit fat tails and occasional volatility clustering, meaning extreme moves occur more frequently than a simple Gaussian model would imply. This means the true probability of outcomes outside my stated ranges is likely somewhat higher than the nominal 10%, especially at the one-month horizon where there is more time for non-linear dynamics — such as momentum cascades or sentiment shifts — to take hold.
